tldr: Survey respondents identify workforce readiness and childcare access as critical barriers, alongside business climate friction (permitting delays, cumulative taxes, regulatory complexity). Business owners express concerns about specific policies: QSBS tax-incentive removal, Climate Protection Program compliance costs, and land-use restrictions limiting expansion. Rural communities report feeling excluded from economic planning. Common requests: streamlined permitting, support for small/local businesses, preschool/K-12 funding, higher wages in lower-paid sectors, and coordinated state agency leadership.

bullets.text: Childcare and preschool availability cited as major barrier to workforce participation, especially for women; respondents advocate free/subsidized programs like Preschool for All and NYC model

QSBS (Qualified Small Business Stock) tax incentive removal described as existential threat to startup ecosystem and founder retention; Julie Scotland reports considering out-of-state move due to tax implications
Climate Protection Program compliance costs cited as unsustainable; Lignetics reports $13,000/month per plant ($156,000 annually) in CPP costs with threat of plant closure if increases continue

Outdoor recreation industry generates $16 billion in annual consumer spending and approximately 192,000 full- and part-time jobs; Oregon Wild advocates for mature/old-growth forest protections and climate solutions investment
Rural communities report inadequate representation in economic planning; Pamela advocates for rural inclusion in Governor's plan execution and local economic development hubs as resource centers

Permitting delays, regulatory complexity, and cumulative local/state/county tax layering identified as primary friction points; Springfield Chamber survey shows employers cite public safety (65%), state taxes (35%), reduced regulations (34%) as priorities

Wage stagnation in lower-paid sectors (caregiving, healthcare, childcare) limits career advancement for women and working families; multiple respondents advocate increased minimum wages and sector-specific wage boosts

Albert LePage proposes reframing economic policy around 'well-being economy' metrics (mental health, social capital, ecological integrity) instead of growth-only measures; cites global models and calls for integrated workforce/business/land-use strategy

State workforce and economic development systems criticized as siloed, underfunded, and misaligned; calls for unified 'One Oregon' concept, single-entry support portals, and integrated data systems connecting education through employment

Latino Network and BIPOC respondents cite lack of capacity, funding, and leadership representation in state agencies and workforce programs; advocate for statewide strategy and multi-year funding for Latine-led business/workforce development
